Back in the 70s, a teenager got pulled into something that doesn't show up in any success book: an organization called the Brotherhood.

It worked alongside Skull and Bones out of Yale, Bohemian Grove, the Bilderberg Group, and the highest levels of Freemasonry. Inside those rooms, the training wasn't positive thinking or hustle culture — it was how to move and manipulate energy with the power of the mind, how to actually create reality with it. None of that gets taught in the mainstream. It's taught behind closed doors, on purpose.

Comment RISE and I'll send you what else was in that training.

Everything in the personal growth world tells you to practice gratitude first. Here's the step almost nobody teaches, and it comes before the gratitude: you have to hate where you are right now.

Negative energy contracts, and that contraction is what gives you the force to actually move — like Darth Vader's "your anger makes you focus," except real. There's an old hound dog that whines every few minutes because he's lying on a nail. He never moves. Why? Because it doesn't hurt quite enough yet. The pain has to get big enough that staying still is worse than changing.

An electron is a wave — until something observes it, and then it becomes a particle. That's not metaphor, that's physics. And it's exactly how a thought turns into a thing.

A thought starts as a wave. Focus on it specifically enough and it becomes a particle in your own energy field — something other people can actually pick up on. "I can look at somebody on the phone and just know: red Porsche. They ask how I knew. It's right there in your field, clear as a bell." But to pull it fully into the physical world, there's one more step: you have to write it down.

Comment RISE and I'll send you the rest of the formula.

Picture exactly what you want, and feel right now as if you already have it. That part sounds simple. It's also where almost everyone gets it wrong.

Here's the part they skip: once you're feeling it, you have to release the attachment to actually getting it. Say it and mean it — it's totally fine if this never happens — while keeping that same feeling going. The moment you genuinely stop needing it, and you're still feeling as good as if you had it, that's the moment people say it showed up when they least expected it. That's the release doing its job.

Comment RISE and I'll send you how to actually practice this.

Mike Pompeo ballooned up while he was Secretary of State. Later, seeing him in person, he looked so different it was unrecognizable — lean, in phenomenal shape.

His own explanation: he stepped out of the shower, looked in the mirror, and felt disgusted with what he saw. Not for a second — he stood there with that feeling for five full minutes. And that was the whole trigger. That same day, not the next day, he started exercising and changed his diet. One moment of real disgust did more than years of good intentions ever did.

Comment RISE and I'll send you the rest of the mechanism.

Writing your goal down is step one. Here's the step after it that almost nobody does: go physically touch the thing.

Want a car? Go to the dealership, sit in it, touch the wheel, smell the interior. Want a Rolex? Go put it on your wrist and have someone take a photo of you wearing it. It sounds like a gimmick, but it isn't — touching something in the physical universe changes your energy around it, and that's what actually speeds up how fast it shows up in your life.

Comment RISE and I'll send you the rest of the technique.

Look at anyone who's made real money, going all the way back to Andrew Carnegie and Henry Ford, up through Elon Musk and Steve Jobs. Every single one of them is part of something: a private club, a secret society, an association.

At the smaller end it's a Rotary Club or a Young Presidents' Organization. At the top, it's rooms most people never hear the name of. Why does it matter so much? Because there's a connection running through your own family line, through your DNA, and who you're energetically linked to pulls you up or drags you down.

Every genuinely successful person belongs to a group that pulls for them, and they pull for everyone else in it. That energetic support, not just the favors or the phone calls, is what actually makes the difference.

CEOs running billion-dollar companies do this constantly: they meet once a month, quietly, in someone's home or the back room of a restaurant.
